blocks.prompt: The River Horse That Cannot Swim
blocks.text: A hippo spends its whole day in the river. Its eyes, ears, and nose sit on top of its head. That way it can see, hear, and breathe while the rest of it stays under the water. A hippo cannot swim. It is too heavy to float. So it walks along the bottom of the river, and it pushes off with its feet to bounce back up. When the sun goes down, the hippo walks out onto the grass. It eats grass all night long. A hippo eats grass and nothing else, even though its mouth is bigger than a bathtub.

blocks.prompt: The River Horse That Cannot Swim
blocks.text: The word hippopotamus comes from two old Greek words that mean river horse. It is a good name. A hippo spends up to sixteen hours a day in the water. But here is the strange part. A hippo cannot swim. Its body is too heavy and too dense to float, so it sinks. Instead of swimming, a hippo walks along the river bottom. When it wants to come up, it pushes off the mud with its feet and drifts back to the surface like a slow balloon. A hippo's eyes, ears, and nostrils all sit in a line on top of its head. It can rest with its whole body hidden and still watch the riverbank. When it dives, its nostrils squeeze shut and its ears fold flat. Hippos even sleep in the water. A sleeping hippo floats up to breathe without waking, then sinks again. It has been doing this its whole life and never has to think about it. At night the hippo climbs out and eats grass. Nothing but grass.

blocks.prompt: The Sunscreen the Hippo Makes Itself
blocks.text: Hippopotamus means river horse in ancient Greek, but the hippo's closest living relatives are not horses at all. They are whales and dolphins. Around fifty-five million years ago, a group of hoofed animals waded into the water and never really came back out. One branch kept going and became whales. Another branch stopped halfway and became hippos. You can see the family resemblance if you know where to look. A hippo has almost no hair. It gives birth underwater, and its calf nurses underwater. Its eyes, ears, and nostrils are stacked along the top of its skull so it can float almost invisibly. And yet a hippo cannot swim. It is denser than water, so it sinks straight to the bottom. What looks like swimming is really a slow bounce. The hippo pushes off the riverbed, glides up, sinks, and pushes off again. Hippo skin has another problem. It is thin, and it dries out fast in the African sun. So the hippo makes its own sunscreen. Glands under the skin ooze a thick fluid that starts clear, turns pink, then dries to a rusty brown. People used to call it blood sweat. It is neither blood nor sweat. It blocks sunlight and it kills bacteria, which helps the cuts hippos give each other heal in dirty water. Every evening the hippo hauls itself onto land and walks for kilometers, cropping grass with lips as wide as a doormat. It eats around forty kilograms of grass in a night, then returns to the same stretch of river before the sun can find it.

blocks.prompt: The Heaviest Gardener in Africa
blocks.text: Nothing about a hippopotamus makes sense until you stop thinking of it as a land animal. A big male common hippo weighs around three thousand kilograms, roughly the weight of a small truck. He carries that weight on short legs, and he carries it into the water at dawn and holds it there for up to sixteen hours. He is not swimming. A hippo is denser than water and sinks. What it does instead is walk, and where the water deepens it bounces: a push off the riverbed, a long slow glide upward, a sink, another push. Underwater, a hippo moves with a grace it can never manage on land. Everything on its head is arranged for that life. Eyes, ears, and nostrils sit along one plane on top of the skull, so a hippo can breathe and watch a riverbank while the other three thousand kilograms stay invisible. On a dive the nostrils clamp shut and the ears fold in. A sleeping hippo will rise, take a breath, and sink again without waking. The reflex runs whether the animal is paying attention or not. The water is not a hunting ground. Hippos eat grass, and only grass. The famous yawn, that vast pink hinge of a mouth swinging open past a right angle, is not tiredness and not hunger. It is a threat, and the teeth on display are the argument. Hippos are territorial, and when the display fails, males fight with those tusks in earnest. So why stay in the river at all? Because hippo skin is thin, nearly hairless, and loses water so fast that a hippo left in full sun would dehydrate. The river is not a habitat so much as a shelter. To survive the hours it must spend in the open, the hippo secretes a reddish oily fluid from glands in its skin, a substance that absorbs ultraviolet light and discourages bacteria. It is sunscreen and antiseptic, made by the animal wearing it. The grass comes at night. A hippo hauls out after dark, walks several kilometers, and mows down roughly forty kilograms of grass with lips built like a shovel. Then it carries all of that back into the river and, over the following day, releases it there. Biologists have measured what this does. Hippos move silicon and other nutrients from the grassland into the water, feeding the microscopic algae at the base of the whole river food web. The river's smallest life is fed by the river's largest animal, which eats nothing in the river at all.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Hippopotamus amphibius: third largest land mammal
Split from the whale lineage roughly 55 million years ago
Negatively buoyant: it walks and bounces, it does not swim
Hipposudoric acid absorbs UV and inhibits bacteria
Gape opens past 150 degrees as a threat display
Mara River studies: hippos move silicon to feed diatoms

blocks.prompt: The River Horse: Built by Water, Fed by Grass
blocks.text: The hippopotamus is a puzzle assembled from parts that seem to disagree. It is the third largest land mammal alive, and it can barely tolerate land. It has the mouth of a monster and the diet of a lawnmower. Its name, from the Greek hippopotamos, means river horse, and its closest living relatives are neither rivers nor horses but whales. That last fact is the key to the rest. Somewhere around fifty-five million years ago, a lineage of hoofed mammals moved into the water. One branch kept going and became the cetaceans, the whales and dolphins that never returned. Another branch stopped halfway and became the hippos. The evidence is still written on the animal. Hippos are almost hairless. They give birth underwater, their calves nurse underwater, and they call to each other with clicks and rumbles that carry through water and air at once. A hippo is a mammal caught mid-sentence between two worlds. Consider what it does with buoyancy. A hippo does not float. Its bones are dense and its body is heavy, so a hippo placed in deep water sinks, which sounds like a design failure until you watch one. It walks the riverbed. Where the water deepens it bounces, pushing off the bottom, gliding upward in a slow arc, settling, pushing again. On land a three thousand kilogram hippo is a heavy, unhappy thing that runs in short furious bursts. Underwater it is nearly weightless and almost graceful. It has not failed to swim. It has stopped needing to. Its skull is arranged around the same logic. Eyes, ears, and nostrils sit in a single plane along the top of the head, so a hippo can watch a riverbank, hear a rival, and breathe with nothing else showing. Diving closes the nostrils and folds the ears. A sleeping hippo surfaces, breathes, and sinks again without waking, an automatic reflex that runs for a lifetime without a single conscious decision. None of this is hunting equipment. Hippos are herbivores, and their fights are with each other. The enormous gape, opening past a right angle to display tusks that can exceed half a meter, is a threat, a way of settling a territorial dispute by showing what the alternative would cost. When the display fails, males fight, and the wounds are real. The river itself is not where the hippo feeds. It is where the hippo hides from the sun. Hippo skin is thin and nearly hairless, and it loses water so quickly that a hippo stranded in daylight would dehydrate. To survive the exposure it cannot avoid, the animal secretes a viscous fluid from glands in its skin. The fluid starts colorless, reddens within minutes, and dries brown. Early observers called it blood sweat, and it is neither. It absorbs ultraviolet light and it inhibits bacteria: a sunscreen and an antiseptic, manufactured and worn by the same animal. Food arrives at night. A hippo hauls out after dark, walks several kilometers on well-worn trails, and crops roughly forty kilograms of grass using lips shaped like a shovel. Before dawn it returns to the same water. This is where the animal stops being merely strange and starts being important. Everything it eats on the grassland, it deposits in the river. Researchers working on the Mara River in Kenya measured the transfer and found hippos moving hundreds of kilograms of silicon into the water every day, silicon that diatoms, the microscopic algae at the base of the food web, cannot build their glassy shells without. So the river's smallest organisms are fed by the river's largest animal, which eats nothing in the river at all. Remove the hippos and the grass stays on the grassland, and the water slowly becomes something else. The animal that cannot swim turns out to be holding the river up.
